projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Employee Management Module
projects.scope: Core employee records, org hierarchy, and role-based access.
projects.context: A mid-sized enterprise needed to digitize its HR operations. I was one of [X] front-end developers on a team building four interconnected Angular applications. This module holds the employee records every other module depends on.
projects.challenge: Employee data feeds every other HR app, so the data model and permissions had to be right from the start. Four apps with different business scopes could not each rebuild the same forms, tables and access rules.
solution: Shared TypeScript interfaces for employee and org-unit models, reused across all four apps.
A recursive tree component for the org hierarchy, built on the shared UI library.
Route guards plus a structural directive that shows or hides UI by role and permission.
role: Built reusable form, table and tree components.
Implemented the role-based access layer (guards and directive).
Wrote the API service layer for employee endpoints.
Reviewed pull requests and helped keep the module structure consistent.
outcome: Reduced new-feature development time by ~X% through component reuse.
Delivered consistent UX across four apps on one codebase.
lessons: I would define the permission model as a shared contract earlier, before building screens.
I would add visual regression tests for the shared components from the first sprint.

projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Attendance Management Module
projects.scope: Real-time attendance tracking and reporting dashboards.
projects.context: The same HR platform needed a way to track attendance across the organization and report on it. I was one of [X] front-end developers working on this module alongside the other three apps.
projects.challenge: Attendance data changes constantly and managers need fast, readable summaries. The screens had to stay responsive with large lists and frequent updates.
solution: Attendance events flow through RxJS streams into a service-level store; views subscribe with the async pipe.
Reusable filter and date-range components shared with the other modules.
Dashboard widgets built as small presentational components fed by one data stream.
role: Implemented the stream-based data layer for attendance records.
Optimized list rendering with OnPush change detection and trackBy.
Contributed shared filter components to the common library.
outcome: Reduced new-feature development time by ~X% through component reuse.
Delivered consistent UX across four apps on one codebase.
lessons: I would agree on update frequency and data shape with the back end before building the stream layer.
I would add a shared loading and empty-state pattern sooner.

projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Training Management Module
projects.scope: Multi-step training workflows with clear progress states.
projects.context: HR teams needed to plan, assign and follow up on employee training. I was one of [X] front-end developers on this module as part of the four-app platform.
projects.challenge: Training requests move through several steps and states. Users needed to always know where an item stands and what to do next.
solution: A reusable stepper workflow built on Angular Material, with per-step validation.
Explicit progress states modeled as TypeScript union types, so invalid states cannot compile.
Shared status badge and timeline components used across the platform.
role: Built the multi-step forms and workflow screens.
Modeled workflow states and transitions in TypeScript.
Created the status and progress components now shared with other apps.
outcome: Reduced new-feature development time by ~X% through component reuse.
Delivered consistent UX across four apps on one codebase.
lessons: I would document the workflow state model in the repo for the next developer.
I would test each transition with unit tests earlier.

projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Workload Management Module
projects.context: Managers needed a clear view of team workload and available capacity. I was one of [X] front-end developers building this module with the rest of the platform.
projects.challenge: Capacity data is dense. The interface had to make over- and under-allocation obvious at a glance without overwhelming the user.
solution: Chart and heat-map components wrapped in the shared UI library with a consistent API.
Derived values (utilization, remaining capacity) computed in services, not in templates.
Lazy-loaded the visualization code so it only downloads when the module opens.
role: Implemented the services that calculate capacity and utilization.
Handled lazy loading and bundle-size checks for the module.
outcome: Reduced new-feature development time by ~X% through component reuse.
Delivered consistent UX across four apps on one codebase.
lessons: I would set accessibility rules for charts (text alternatives, color contrast) at the start.
I would profile large datasets earlier to choose between SVG and canvas.

architecture.title: Shared component library
architecture.text: Tables, forms, dialogs, status badges and charts live in one shared module with a stable API. Feature modules compose them instead of rebuilding them.

architecture.title: Service layer and API abstraction
architecture.text: Components never call HttpClient directly. A typed ApiService handles base URL and errors, and feature services build on it.

architecture.title: RxJS state management
architecture.text: Services expose observables. Components subscribe with the async pipe, so subscriptions clean themselves up and state flows one way.

architecture.title: Lazy loading and module structure
architecture.text: Code is split into core, shared and feature areas. Each feature is lazy-loaded by route, so users download only what they open.
